metadata.title: How to square the circle of voluntary participation in controlled samples?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2024 in Latvia as the sampling frame and then conducts a three-phase follow-up (coordinator online survey; purposive selection of schools by teacher participation rates; teacher surveys and principal interviews). The manuscript does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights (e.g., student/teacher design weights) or any replicate-weight variance estimation, and it does not provide weight variable names. Quantitative analyses are limited to descriptive statistics, correlations, and Mann–Whitney U tests, so the paper does not describe PV-based scaling or achievement-score estimation procedures. For replication with ILSA microdata, analysts should apply the official TALIS complex survey design weights when estimating population-representative quantities, but this paper’s reported outcomes are primarily participation-rate distributions and perceptions rather than PV-based achievement scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not model cognitive achievement outcomes generated via PVs. The dependent variables are participation rates (e.g., early/late/non-response proportions) and survey/interview perceptions about survey design and participation, which are not PV-based achievement scales. Missing data handling is described as excluding cases with missing values using pairwise deletion for quantitative comparisons.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Quantitative follow-up data were collected in three phases after TALIS 2024 in Latvia. Phase 1: all 216 TALIS 2024 school coordinators were invited to complete an online follow-up survey; 119 responded. Phase 2: schools were ranked by teacher participation rates; 10 lowest-rate schools (≤75%) and 10 highest-rate schools (100%) were invited (20 approached); 11 principals consented and 9 declined/did not respond. Phase 3: teachers from the 11 selected schools were purposively sampled to represent both TALIS 2024 respondents and non-respondents: from low-response schools, 5 survey participants and 5 non-participants; from high-response schools, 10 survey participants. This yielded a potential sample of 110 teachers (75 respondents, 35 non-respondents) and an achieved sample of 93 teachers (66 respondents, 27 non-respondents). Participation was voluntary and confidential; surveys were administered in printed and online formats mirroring coordinator instruments. Quantitative analyses excluded cases with missing values using pairwise deletion.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2024 in Latvia the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper is a mixed-methods follow-up study to TALIS 2024 in Latvia, focusing on how voluntary teacher participation can be achieved under school-level participation requirements. It reports participation dynamics using coordinator-reported teacher participation categories (early birds, late comers, non-respondents) and compares perceptions across groups of schools and teachers with different participation patterns. Quantitatively, it finds that 17% of teachers responded in the first week, 4% in the last week, and 10% did not log into the survey system; reminders were associated with up to a 4% increase in completed questionnaires. It also reports that voluntary participation correlates positively with immediate participation (correlation 0.6, p<0.001) and that postponement with increasing reminders is negatively associated with voluntary participation (correlation −0.6, p<0.001). The study uses descriptive statistics, correlations, and Mann–Whitney U tests, with pairwise deletion for missing values, and does not train or evaluate machine learning models or PV-based achievement outcomes. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification study: the manuscript reports mixed-methods qualitative thematic analysis and descriptive/association tests (correlations, Mann–Whitney U) about survey participation and perceptions. Therefore, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV handling, and no predictive target variables with model performance metrics. The absence of main_findings rows is consistent with the paper’s design as a participation/attitudes study rather than an ML-based ILSA achievement modeling paper.
